headline: NASA's Swift telescope falls to Earth after 22 years

sources.title: 3,200-pound space telescope plunges back to Earth after 22 years in orbit (CBS News)
NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt (Space.com)
A storied NASA observatory could be weeks away from falling to Earth after failed rescue attempt (CNN via KRDO)
Nasa telescope launched in 2004 to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission (The Guardian)

chunks.text: NASA's Swift space telescope was built to work for just two years. It {{held up}} for almost 22 years. On November 4, 2026, it fell from [[orbit]], its path around Earth. The U.S. Space Force [[confirmed]] that it {{came down}} over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia. NASA expected most of the 3,200-pound telescope to {{burn up}} high above Earth. Some pieces may have [[survived]] the fall.

verbs.correct: To keep working well over time
verbs.why: Good boots hold up for many years. Cheap phones rarely hold up after a few falls. Swift was built to work for just two years, but it held up for almost 22 years.
Snow comes down all night in the mountains. Old weather balloons come down in empty fields. The telescope came down over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia.

verbs.correct: To be destroyed by great heat
verbs.wrong: To send a last signal to Earth
verbs.why: Most small space rocks burn up in the air. Old papers burn up quickly in a hot fire. NASA expected most of the telescope to burn up high above Earth.

chunks.text: Swift, a machine with three telescopes [[on board]], {{blasted off}} in November 2004. Its main job was to study gamma-ray bursts, the most [[powerful explosions]] in space. Some [[bursts]] last less than a second, so speed [[mattered]]. Swift could {{zero in on}} a burst's spot in about a minute, before its glow was gone. It {{picked up}} more than 2,000 bursts and studied 1,400 stars that {{blew up}}. It [[alerted]] other telescopes to take a closer look.

verbs.correct: To leave the ground at great speed
verbs.wrong: To circle the moon and return home
verbs.why: The astronauts blast off at dawn. Rockets blast off from this site every month. Swift blasted off in November 2004 with three telescopes on board.

verbs.correct: To find one exact spot and aim there
verbs.wrong: To fly quickly past a small star
verbs.why: Security cameras zero in on the front door. The news camera zeroes in on the winner. Swift could zero in on a burst's spot in about a minute.

verbs.correct: To find a signal using equipment
verbs.wrong: To send a warning to scientists
verbs.why: My old radio picks up stations from far away. This phone picks up a signal almost everywhere. Swift picked up more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts.

verbs.wrong: To circle a distant black hole
verbs.why: Old gas tanks sometimes blow up in a fire. Fireworks blow up high in the sky. Swift studied 1,400 stars that blew up.

chunks.text: [[Thin air]] high above Earth pulled Swift lower for years. Strong activity on the sun made that air spread higher and {{sped up}} the fall. In 2025, NASA hired a [[private company]] to save the telescope. In July 2026, the company {{sent up}} a robot [[spacecraft]] to push Swift higher. The robot soon {{ran into}} trouble and began to spin [[out of control]]. Fixing that problem {{used up}} the fuel it needed for the [[rescue]]. In August 2026, NASA and the company {{called off}} the rescue.

verbs.wrong: To make a machine easier to fix
verbs.why: Warm weather speeds up plant growth. A new computer speeds up my work. Strong activity on the sun sped up the telescope's fall.

verbs.correct: To launch something high in the sky
verbs.wrong: To test something on the ground
verbs.why: The weather service sends up balloons every day. The space agency sends up a new satellite each year. In July 2026, the company sent up a robot spacecraft to push Swift higher.

verbs.wrong: To hire a new business partner
verbs.why: Small companies often run into money problems. New drivers run into trouble on icy roads. The robot soon ran into trouble and began to spin out of control.

verbs.correct: To finish all of a supply
verbs.wrong: To check how much is left
verbs.why: Long video calls use up my phone battery. We use up all the milk in two days. Fixing the robot's problem used up the fuel it needed for the rescue.

verbs.correct: To decide that something will not happen
verbs.wrong: To give a rescue team a new date
verbs.why: Schools call off classes when the snow is heavy. Teams call off games in bad storms. In August 2026, NASA and the company called off the rescue.

chunks.text: Swift {{wrapped up}} its last science work on October 20, 2026. NASA had put the [[odds]] of falling pieces hurting anyone at about 1 in 2,100. Such falls are common. A 2025 report found at least three large objects, such as [[dead satellites]], fall to Earth every day [[on average]]. NASA says the failed rescue taught [[useful lessons]]. Scientists are still trying to {{figure out}} how to [[replace]] Swift's work.

verbs.correct: To finish a piece of work
verbs.wrong: To study a new part of space
verbs.why: Most teachers wrap up the lesson with a short quiz. Our team wraps up each meeting by noon. Swift wrapped up its last science work on October 20, 2026.

verbs.wrong: To build a new kind of telescope
verbs.why: Kids figure out new phones very fast. Good mechanics figure out what is wrong with a car. Scientists are still trying to figure out how to replace Swift's work.

mainIdea.s: A NASA telescope built for two years kept working for almost 22, then fell from orbit in November 2026. A private rescue attempt had failed, and scientists still need a way to replace its work.
mainIdea.why: Swift held up far longer than planned, then came down on November 4, 2026. The rescue was called off, and scientists are still trying to figure out how to replace its work.

mainIdea.s: Swift finally came down because a robot spacecraft crashed into it during a mission. NASA had planned to bring the old machine home so that engineers could study how it held up in space.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the robot never touched Swift. Thin air and activity on the sun pulled the telescope lower, and the rescue was called off in August 2026.

mainIdea.s: NASA has launched a new telescope to search for gamma-ray bursts near distant galaxies. Engineers expect this modern observatory to start returning its first pictures early next spring.
mainIdea.why: This is about an old telescope ending its work, not a new one starting. Swift wrapped up its last science work on October 20, 2026.

tf.s: The Swift telescope held up for far longer than NASA planned.
tf.why: It was built to work for just two years, and it held up for almost 22 years.

tf.s: The rescue mission saved Swift and pushed it to a higher orbit.
tf.why: The robot spacecraft ran into trouble, and NASA and the company called off the rescue.

tf.s: NASA expected most of the telescope to burn up high above Earth.
tf.why: Most of it was expected to burn up, but some pieces may have survived.

tf.s: Swift picked up very few of the bursts it was built to study.
tf.why: Swift picked up more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts during its long life.

tf.s: Strong activity on the sun slowed Swift's fall to Earth.
tf.why: Activity on the sun made thin air spread higher, and that sped up the fall.

tf.s: Scientists are still trying to figure out how to replace Swift's work.
tf.why: Swift has stopped working, and scientists have to figure out how to do that job.

lines.text: Did you see that NASA's Swift telescope {{came down}} on November 4?
I saw something about it. Wasn't it really old?
Almost 22 years old. It was only built to work for two years.
Wow, it really {{held up}}. I'd call that [[a good run]].
For sure. It {{picked up}} more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, and it could {{zero in on}} one in about a minute.
Impressive. So why did it fall?
Thin air kept pulling it lower, and activity on the sun {{sped up}} the fall.
Well, [[nothing lasts forever]]. Didn't someone try to save it?
Yes. A private company {{sent up}} a robot, but it soon {{ran into}} trouble.
So what happened to the rescue?
Fixing the problem {{used up}} the fuel it needed, so they {{called off}} the rescue.
[[Better luck next time]], I guess. What about falling pieces?
It was never going to reach the ground [[in one piece]]. NASA expected most of it to {{burn up}}.
NASA said about 1 in 2,100. I wouldn't [[lose sleep over]] it.
Me either. So who does Swift's job now?
Scientists are still trying to {{figure out}} how to replace it.
